journeyIntro: For colleagues, managers and teammates. Practise clear requests, feedback and respectful collaboration.

lessons.title: Make Clear Requests
lessons.summary: Say what you need without guessing games.

steps.title: Vague asks get vague results
steps.body: “Can you send that over at some point?” leaves everyone guessing. A clear request says what you need, by when and, ideally, why it matters.

steps.prompt: You need a teammate’s sales figures to finish a report, and they haven’t arrived. What do you send?

options.text: “You’re holding the whole report up.”
options.why: Blame puts them on the back foot and doesn’t tell them what you actually need or when.

options.text: Say nothing and hope they remember.
options.why: They may not know it’s urgent, and you’ll be left scrambling at the deadline.

options.text: “Could you send the Q3 figures by Thursday noon? I need them for Friday’s report.”
options.why: It names the exact thing, the deadline and the reason, so it’s easy to prioritise.

steps.prompt: Add the deadline.
steps.after: so I can finish the report?
steps.why: A specific time removes the guesswork and makes the request easy to plan around.

steps.prompt: What makes asking colleagues for things hard for you?
options: Feeling I should do it all
steps.reply: Common at work. A clear, polite request is a kindness: it saves everyone time.

steps.prompt: Clear request or vague one?

cards.text: “Could you send the Q3 numbers by 3pm today?”
“Whenever you get a chance…”
“Can someone look at this?”
“Sam, could you review slides 4–6 by Friday?”
“Need that thing asap”

steps.why: Clear requests name who, what and when, so people can say yes and actually deliver.

steps.body: Make one work request today that says exactly what you need, by when and why.

lessons.title: Write Better Emails
lessons.summary: Lead with the point, then the detail.

steps.title: Busy people skim
steps.body: Most people read the first two lines of an email. Put what you need, and by when, at the top. The background can follow for anyone who wants it.

steps.prompt: You need your manager to approve a budget by Thursday. How should your email start?

options.text: “Could you approve the events budget by Thursday? Details below.”
options.why: The ask and deadline are right at the top, so it can’t be missed.

options.text: A long recap of the project so far, with the ask at the end.
options.why: The request may never be read if they stop after a paragraph.

options.text: “Hi, hope you’re well! Just checking in.”
options.why: Friendly, but it hides why you’re writing.

steps.prompt: Lead with the ask.
steps.why: A clear verb and a deadline up front make your email easy to act on.

steps.prompt: What slows your emails down most?
steps.reply: Fixing just that one habit can make your emails noticeably quicker to act on.

steps.prompt: Clear email habit, or confusing one?

cards.text: Subject: “Approval needed by Thu: events budget”
Subject: “Quick question”
One ask per email
Five questions buried in paragraphs
Bullet points for key details

steps.why: Clear emails put the ask first and make details easy to scan, so people can respond quickly.

steps.body: Rewrite your next work email so the ask and deadline are in the first line.

lessons.title: Speak Up in Meetings
lessons.summary: Your ideas count. Share them clearly.

steps.title: Good ideas need a voice
steps.body: Many people stay quiet in meetings, worried they’ll sound silly. A short, clear point, “I’d suggest X because Y”, is often exactly what the room needs.

steps.prompt: In a meeting, you have an idea that could save time, but you’re nervous to speak up. What’s best?

options.text: Stay quiet and email it to someone later.
options.why: It might never get heard, or someone else may get the credit.

options.text: “Can I add something? We could reuse last year’s template, which would save a week.”
options.why: Short, clear and tied to a benefit, which makes it easy to consider.

options.text: Wait until the very end of the meeting.
options.why: By then, decisions may already be made.

steps.prompt: A clear way in.
steps.why: A polite opener gives you the floor without interrupting.

steps.prompt: What stops you speaking up in meetings?
steps.reply: Preparing one point before the meeting makes it much easier to share.

steps.prompt: Making a point in a meeting. Put these in order.
steps.why: Preparation and good timing help you speak confidently; asking for thoughts makes it a team discussion.

steps.body: Prepare one point before your next meeting and share it during the discussion.

lessons.title: Listen in Meetings
lessons.summary: Understand the point before replying.

steps.title: Waiting to talk isn’t listening
steps.body: In meetings it’s easy to spend someone’s whole point preparing your reply. Then you answer what you expected them to say, not what they said.

steps.prompt: In a planning meeting, a colleague raises concerns about your launch plan. What’s the most useful response?

options.text: Cut in to defend the plan before they finish.
options.why: Interrupting can make you look defensive and you may miss a concern that’s genuinely useful.

options.text: Check your phone until they’re done.
options.why: Others notice, and the colleague may feel their input doesn’t matter to you.

options.text: “So your main worry is that two weeks isn’t enough for testing?”
options.why: Summarising checks you’ve understood and shows you take their concern seriously.

steps.title: Summarise, then respond
steps.body: A quick summary like “So you’re saying…” takes seconds. It catches misunderstandings early and often calms a tense meeting.

steps.prompt: Check you understood.
steps.why: It reflects their point fairly without shrinking or exaggerating it.

steps.prompt: When do you find it hardest to listen at work?
steps.reply: Knowing that moment helps. Try a quick summary there before you respond.

steps.title: A worried message

lines.text: Honestly, I’m not sure the new booking process is going to work.

steps.prompt: You designed the process. Reply:

options.text: It’s only been a week, give it time.
options.why: Dismissing it means you lose useful feedback, and she may stop raising issues.

options.text: It worked fine in testing.
options.why: Defending the work closes the door before you’ve heard what’s going wrong.

options.text: Thanks for flagging. What are clients getting stuck on?
options.reaction: Mostly step two. I’ll send you some examples!
options.why: Thanking her and asking for specifics turns a worry into something you can fix together.

steps.body: In your next meeting, summarise one colleague’s point in a sentence before giving your own view.

lessons.title: Clarify Before You Start
lessons.summary: A few questions now save hours later.

steps.title: Check you’ve understood
steps.body: It’s tempting to nod and get started. But a quick “So the goal is…, by…, for…?” catches misunderstandings before they cost you days of work.

steps.prompt: Your manager asks for “a quick report on sales” and walks off. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Start writing a full report straight away.
options.why: You might spend days on something different from what they need.

options.text: Ask a colleague what they think it means.
options.why: They’re guessing too.

options.text: “Quick check: which months, who’s it for, and when do you need it?”
options.why: Three quick questions make sure you build the right thing.

steps.prompt: Play it back.
steps.after: , you need this by Friday for the board?
steps.why: Playing back the task in your words catches mix-ups early.

steps.prompt: How often do you ask questions before starting a task?
steps.reply: Asking a little more upfront often saves a lot of rework later.

steps.prompt: Match each vague ask with a clarifying question.
steps.why: Clarifying questions turn vague requests into clear tasks, saving everyone time and frustration.

steps.body: Before starting your next task, play back the goal and deadline to whoever asked.

lessons.title: Hear the Quiet Voices
lessons.summary: The best ideas aren’t always the loudest.

steps.title: Quiet doesn’t mean empty
steps.body: In most meetings, a few people do most of the talking. Inviting quieter colleagues in, by name and kindly, often brings out the most thoughtful ideas.

steps.prompt: In your team meeting, Aisha hasn’t spoken but looks like she has thoughts. What’s best?

options.text: Let her be. She’ll speak if she wants to.
options.why: Some people need an invitation before they feel able to speak.

options.text: “Aisha, you know this area well. What do you think?”
options.why: A warm, specific invite makes it easy for her to contribute.

options.text: “Aisha, why are you so quiet?”
options.why: Pointing out quietness can make someone feel put on the spot.

steps.prompt: Invite them in.
steps.why: A simple invitation shows their view is valued.

steps.prompt: In meetings, you’re usually…
steps.reply: Whichever you are, making room for others helps the whole team.

steps.prompt: Includes quieter voices, or shuts them out?

cards.text: Going round the table for views
Talking over someone mid-sentence
Sharing the agenda in advance
Deciding before everyone has spoken
Inviting written ideas after the meeting

steps.why: Small habits like asking everyone and sharing agendas early help quieter colleagues contribute their best ideas.

steps.body: In your next meeting, warmly invite one quieter person to share their view.

lessons.title: Build Small Connections
lessons.summary: Warmth can fit into a busy workday.

steps.title: Warmth makes work work
steps.body: Teams that feel connected tend to share problems sooner and help each other more. It doesn’t take team-building days, just small, regular warmth.

steps.prompt: A new person joins your project team this week. What’s the most helpful thing you can do?

options.text: Leave it to their manager to sort out.
options.why: Managers help, but a friendly face from the team makes the first week much less lonely.

options.text: Say hello, and show them one thing that’ll make their week easier.
options.why: A warm welcome plus something practical helps them feel included and useful quickly.

options.text: Quiz them on what they know about the project.
options.why: It can feel like a test on day one, when they’re still finding their feet.

steps.prompt: Offer something useful.
steps.why: Practical help in the first days is remembered for a long time.

steps.prompt: How do you usually connect with colleagues?
steps.reply: Any of those can work. One small extra moment of warmth a week goes a long way.

steps.prompt: Match each moment with a small way to connect.
steps.why: Small, timely gestures make work feel friendlier and build the trust teams rely on when things get hard.

steps.body: Offer one colleague a small, practical kindness today: an introduction, a tip or a quick hello.

lessons.title: Remote Team Bonds
lessons.summary: Build connection when you rarely meet in person.

steps.title: Remote work needs small moments
steps.body: Without the coffee machine chats, remote teams can feel lonely and transactional. A few minutes of non-work chat, a funny gif, or a virtual coffee keeps people connected.

steps.prompt: Your fully remote team only ever talks about tasks. What’s an easy way to build connection?

options.text: Start meetings with a two-minute “best thing this week” round.
options.why: Short, light and regular, so everyone gets to know each other a bit.

options.text: Plan a big in-person party once a year.
options.why: Lovely, but rare. Small regular moments matter more.

options.text: Keep it all about work. That’s efficient.
options.why: Efficient now, but teams without connection tend to struggle later.

steps.prompt: A light opener.
steps.why: A positive question warms up the meeting and helps people connect.

steps.prompt: How connected do you feel to your colleagues?
steps.reply: One small habit can help, and you could be the one to start it.

steps.prompt: Match each remote gap with a fix.

pairs.b: A buddy for their first month

steps.why: Small, deliberate rituals replace the natural moments remote teams miss.

steps.body: Invite a colleague you rarely talk to for a 15-minute virtual coffee this week.

lessons.title: Recognise Good Work
lessons.summary: Specific thanks makes people feel valued.

steps.title: Recognition is motivating
steps.body: People who feel their work is noticed are happier and work better together. Specific, timely thanks, “your summary made the meeting so much easier”, means far more than a generic “great job”.

steps.prompt: A colleague stayed late to fix a bug before your launch. What’s the best way to thank them?

options.text: “Thanks.”
options.why: Polite, but it doesn’t show you noticed the effort.

options.text: Assume they know you’re grateful.
options.why: They might not, and unspoken thanks doesn’t motivate anyone.

options.text: “Thank you for staying late on that bug. The launch went smoothly because of you.”
options.why: Specific and public-worthy, so they know exactly what difference they made.

steps.prompt: Name the impact.
steps.before: Your work on the deck really
steps.why: Naming the impact shows their work truly mattered.

steps.prompt: How do you prefer to be recognised?
steps.reply: Others have preferences too. Asking helps your thanks land well.

steps.title: Team chat

lines.text: Took way longer than I thought.

steps.prompt: It was really good. Reply:

options.why: A thumbs up acknowledges it but doesn’t show you valued the work.

options.text: It’s brilliant, Jordan. The summary page made it so easy to follow. Thank you!
options.reaction: Oh, that’s really nice to hear 😊
options.why: Specific praise shows you read it and valued the effort.

options.text: Finally! We were waiting ages.
options.why: It focuses on the delay instead of the good work.

steps.body: Give one colleague specific, sincere thanks for something they did this week.

lessons.title: Protect Focus Time
lessons.summary: Set expectations without disappearing.

steps.title: Available isn’t the same as helpful
steps.body: Answering every message instantly can feel helpful, but constant interruptions make it hard to do your best work, for anyone.

steps.prompt: A colleague keeps calling during your morning focus block, and your own deadline is slipping. What do you do?

options.text: “I’m heads-down until two. Can I call you straight after?”
options.why: It protects your focus, gives a clear time and shows you’re still there for them.

options.text: Keep answering every call and miss your deadline.
options.why: You’ll end up behind and stressed, and they never learn when to reach you.

options.text: Ignore their calls all week.
options.why: Silence can look unhelpful and may cause bigger problems if something is urgent.

steps.title: Make your hours visible
steps.body: Block focus time in your calendar, set a status and say when you’ll be available. Clear signals mean fewer interruptions and fewer hard feelings.

steps.prompt: Offer a time instead.
steps.why: A clear alternative keeps the boundary friendly and the collaboration intact.

steps.prompt: Protecting your focus time. Put these in order.
items: Tell the team when it is
steps.why: Making the boundary visible before you need it means people can respect it without feeling shut out.

steps.body: Block one focus window in your calendar this week and let your team know when you’ll be reachable.

lessons.title: Say No at Work
lessons.summary: A good no protects your best work.

steps.title: Every yes is a no to something
steps.body: Saying yes to every request means your most important work suffers. A helpful no explains your priorities and, where possible, offers an alternative.

steps.prompt: A colleague asks you to join their project committee. You’re already behind on your own deadlines. What’s best?

options.text: Say yes, then struggle to keep up.
options.why: Overcommitting often means doing several things badly.

options.text: “I’d love to, but I need to focus on the launch this month. Could I join next quarter?”
options.why: Honest about priorities, friendly, and offers another option.

options.text: Ignore the message.
options.why: Silence can seem rude and leaves them waiting.

steps.prompt: Explain your priorities.
steps.why: Naming your priority makes your no about the work, not about them.

steps.prompt: What makes saying no at work hardest for you?
options: Not wanting to let people down
steps.reply: A clear, kind no is usually respected far more than an overstretched yes.

steps.prompt: Helpful no, or unhelpful?

cards.text: “Not this week, but I could help next week.”
Saying yes and quietly missing the deadline
“Sam might be a better fit for this.”
“That’s not my job.”
“Which of my tasks should I drop to fit this in?”

steps.why: Helpful nos explain why and offer another route, which keeps relationships strong and work on track.

steps.body: Next time you’re stretched, say no to one request kindly and offer an alternative.

lessons.title: Switch Off After Hours
lessons.summary: Rest makes you better at your job.

steps.title: Always-on wears you out
steps.body: Answering messages late at night can feel helpful, but it sets expectations you’ll struggle to keep, and stops you recovering. Clear after-hours habits protect your energy.

steps.prompt: Your manager sometimes messages at 10pm. You’ve been replying straight away. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Keep replying instantly so they know you’re committed.
options.why: It sets an always-available expectation that’s hard to undo.

options.text: Reply first thing next morning, unless it’s clearly urgent.
options.why: You stay responsive while protecting your evenings.

options.text: Turn off notifications and never mention it.
options.why: Fine for evenings, but agreeing how to reach you in a real emergency helps.

steps.prompt: Set a clear habit.
steps.why: A clear end time helps you rest and helps others know when you’re available.

steps.prompt: How often do you check work messages in the evening?
steps.reply: Even one evening a week fully offline can help you recharge.

steps.prompt: Switching off after work. Put these in order.
steps.why: A short shutdown routine helps your brain let go of work, so you actually rest.

steps.body: Pick an end time for work messages tonight and stick to it.

lessons.title: Be Dependable
lessons.summary: Clear updates matter as much as delivery.

steps.title: Bad news early is good news
steps.body: Everyone misses deadlines sometimes. What damages trust is the surprise. Flag problems early and people can plan around them.

steps.prompt: You realise your part of the project will miss Friday’s deadline. It’s Tuesday. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and see if anyone asks about it.
options.why: By Friday there’s no time left to adjust, and the surprise hurts more than the delay.

options.text: Say it’s nearly done and work late to catch up.
options.why: If it slips anyway, people will doubt your updates in future.

options.text: Tell the team now, explain the impact and suggest a new date.
options.why: An early, honest update with a plan lets others adjust and shows you’re reliable.

steps.prompt: Give an honest update.
steps.after: . I can deliver it on Tuesday.
steps.why: Plain facts plus a new date are the most useful update you can give a team.

steps.prompt: Why is flagging delays hard for you?
steps.reply: Understandable. Early updates usually earn more trust than quietly catching up.

steps.title: One more thing

lines.text: Quick one: could you also take on the client deck this week?

steps.prompt: Your week is already full. Reply:

options.text: Happy to help. To do it well, which should I move: the audit or the training plan?
options.reaction: Good shout, push the training plan to next week.
options.why: You stay helpful and honest about capacity, so you can deliver what you take on.

options.text: Sure, no problem!
options.why: An easy yes now can mean missed deadlines later, which hurts trust more.

options.text: I can’t, I’m swamped.
options.reaction: Oh. Okay, I’ll find someone else.
options.why: Honest, but a flat no misses the chance to work out priorities together.

steps.body: Send one honest progress update this week before anyone asks for it.

lessons.title: Own Your Mistakes
lessons.summary: Owning errors builds more trust than hiding them.

steps.title: Mistakes are normal, hiding them isn’t
steps.body: Everyone gets things wrong at work. What people remember is whether you owned it quickly and helped fix it, or tried to hide it or blame others.

steps.prompt: You sent a client the wrong price list. Nobody has noticed yet. What builds trust?

options.text: Quietly send the right one and hope nobody notices.
options.why: If it’s spotted later, it looks like you hid it.

options.text: Tell your manager now, with the fix you’ve already sent.
options.why: Owning it early, with a solution, shows you’re reliable even when things go wrong.

options.text: Mention that the file names were confusing.
options.why: Blaming the system skips taking responsibility.

steps.prompt: Own it simply.
steps.after: , and here’s how I’ve fixed it.
steps.why: Plain ownership plus a fix is the fastest way to rebuild confidence.

steps.prompt: When you make a mistake at work, you tend to…
steps.reply: Owning it quickly, then letting it go, is what builds a reputation for reliability.

steps.prompt: Match each excuse with ownership.
steps.why: Ownership statements show maturity and make colleagues trust you more, not less.

steps.body: Next time you slip up at work, tell the right person quickly, with a fix ready.

lessons.title: Realistic Deadlines
lessons.summary: Promise dates you can actually hit.

steps.title: Optimistic promises backfire
steps.body: Saying “I’ll have it tomorrow” feels helpful in the moment. But missed deadlines chip away at trust. Adding a little buffer and hitting your date builds a reputation for reliability.

steps.prompt: Your manager asks how long a task will take. You think three days if all goes well. What do you say?

options.text: “Two days, I’ll push hard.”
options.why: Over-promising often leads to late nights and missed deadlines.

options.text: “About four days, to allow for surprises. I’ll update you midweek.”
options.why: Realistic, with a buffer and a check-in, so there are no nasty surprises.

options.text: “Not sure, I’ll let you know.”
options.why: Too vague for them to plan around.

steps.prompt: Build in a buffer.
steps.before: I’ll aim for Thursday, with Friday as the
steps.why: Giving a realistic range helps you deliver on time, every time.

steps.prompt: How accurate are your time estimates?
steps.reply: Most people underestimate. Adding a small buffer is an easy habit to start.

steps.prompt: Builds trust, or risks it?

cards.text: Flagging a delay as soon as you see it
Promising the earliest possible date
Adding a buffer for surprises
Going silent when you’re running late
A midweek progress update

steps.why: Realistic dates and early warnings make you dependable, even when work is unpredictable.

steps.body: For your next task, give a realistic deadline with a small buffer, and a midway update.

lessons.title: Disagree Productively
lessons.summary: Challenge ideas without attacking people.

steps.title: Challenge the plan, not the person
steps.body: Good teams disagree about ideas often, and respectfully. Framing a concern as a question about the work keeps it from feeling personal.

steps.prompt: A teammate proposes a timeline you think is risky. What’s the best way to raise it?

options.text: “What are we assuming about testing time? It feels tight to me.”
options.why: A question about assumptions invites the team to look at the risk together.

options.text: “That timeline’s ridiculous.”
options.why: It attacks the idea’s owner, so the conversation turns defensive instead of useful.

options.text: Agree in the meeting, then complain afterwards.
options.why: The risk goes unaddressed, and complaining privately can erode team trust.

steps.title: When it’s more than disagreement
steps.body: Disagreeing about work is healthy. Bullying, harassment or feeling unsafe is not. Talk to someone you trust, HR or a support service if it happens.

steps.prompt: Frame it as a question.
steps.why: Asking about assumptions focuses on the plan and invites everyone to check it.

steps.prompt: Is there a concern at work you’ve held back? How could you raise it as a question?
About the idea, or about the person?

cards.text: “I’m worried the timeline leaves no buffer.”
“You always rush things.”
“What if testing takes longer than planned?”
“That’s a rookie mistake.”
“Could we compare it with a six-week plan?”

steps.why: Keeping a disagreement on the idea lets you push back hard without damaging the working relationship.

steps.body: Raise one work concern as a question about the plan, rather than a judgement of the person.

lessons.title: Disagree With Your Boss
lessons.summary: Push back respectfully, with reasons.

steps.title: Good managers want honest input
steps.body: Disagreeing with your manager can feel risky. Done respectfully, in private, with facts and a suggested alternative, it usually earns respect rather than trouble.

steps.prompt: Your manager wants to launch next week. You think it needs two more weeks of testing. What’s best?

options.text: Say nothing. It’s their call.
options.why: If problems happen, they may wish you’d spoken up.

options.text: Argue in the team meeting until they change their mind.
options.why: Public pushback can make them defensive.

options.text: Ask for a quick chat: “I’m worried about bugs. Here’s what I found. Two more weeks?”
options.why: Private, specific and solution-focused, which makes it easy to consider.

steps.prompt: Bring evidence.
steps.why: Facts make your concern about the work, not about who’s right.

steps.prompt: How comfortable are you disagreeing with a manager?
steps.reply: Preparing your facts and an alternative makes it much less daunting.

steps.prompt: Disagreeing with your manager. Put these in order.
steps.why: Private, evidence-based pushback with a solution is heard best, and respecting the decision keeps trust intact.

steps.body: If you disagree with a decision at work, raise it privately with one fact and one alternative.

lessons.title: Decide and Commit
lessons.summary: Once it’s decided, back it fully.

steps.title: Disagree, then commit
steps.body: Healthy teams argue openly before a decision. But once it’s made, everyone gets behind it, even those who disagreed. Quietly undermining a decision damages trust.

steps.prompt: Your team chose the plan you argued against. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Do the minimum and wait for it to fail.
options.why: Half-hearted effort can make the plan fail, and hurts your reputation.

options.text: Keep telling colleagues it’s the wrong plan.
options.why: It splits the team and undermines the decision.

options.text: “I had concerns, but I’m on board. Let’s make it work.”
options.why: You stay honest and fully commit, which builds team trust.

steps.prompt: Commit clearly.
steps.before: I see it differently, but I’m fully
steps.why: Committing out loud shows the team you can be relied on, even when you disagree.

steps.prompt: When a decision goes against you, you tend to…
steps.reply: Committing fully, then reviewing results later, is what strong teams do.

steps.prompt: Committing, or quietly undermining?

cards.text: Giving the plan your best effort
“I told you so” when it wobbles
Suggesting a review date to check results
Complaining about it to other teams
Helping others understand the decision

steps.why: Teams succeed when everyone commits once a decision is made, and reviews it fairly afterwards.

steps.body: If a team decision went against you, show your commitment with one helpful action this week.

lessons.title: Give Useful Feedback
lessons.summary: Be specific and kind when something slips.

steps.title: Specific beats general
steps.body: “Be more careful” leaves people unsure what to change. Useful feedback names what happened, why it matters and what would help next time.

steps.prompt: A colleague’s handover notes missed two client deadlines, and you nearly got caught out. What helps most?

options.text: Mention in the team chat that some people are careless.
options.why: Public, vague criticism embarrasses them without saying what to change.

options.text: Tell them which details were missing and suggest a short handover checklist.
options.why: It’s specific about the gap and offers a practical fix, so it’s easy to act on.

options.text: Quietly redo every handover yourself from now on.
options.why: You take on extra work, and they never get the chance to improve.

steps.title: Keep it private and kind
steps.body: Give feedback one to one, soon after it happens, and assume good intent. “I know you were rushed. Could we add deadlines to handovers?”

steps.prompt: Name the specific gap.
steps.before: The handover was helpful, but it
steps.why: Naming exactly what was missing gives them something concrete to fix.

steps.prompt: Giving useful feedback. Put these in order.
steps.why: Facts and impact keep it fair and specific, and agreeing next steps turns criticism into a plan.

steps.body: Give one colleague a piece of specific, kindly worded feedback, with a practical suggestion.

lessons.title: Praise That Lands
lessons.summary: Specific praise teaches and motivates.

steps.title: Praise is feedback too
steps.body: Positive feedback works best when it’s specific: what they did, and why it worked. That way, people know what to keep doing, not just that you’re pleased.

steps.prompt: A junior colleague handled a tough client call really well. Which praise helps most?

options.text: “Great job!”
options.why: Nice, but they won’t know what exactly worked.

options.text: “You stayed calm and summarised their concerns. That’s why they relaxed.”
options.why: Specific praise tells them exactly what to repeat.

options.text: “Not bad for a beginner.”
options.why: The backhanded part takes the shine off.

steps.prompt: Say what worked.
steps.after: the data made it so clear.
steps.why: Naming the action shows exactly what they did well.

steps.prompt: How often do you give colleagues positive feedback?
steps.reply: Specific praise is quick to give and has a big effect. Try it this week.

steps.prompt: Match each vague praise with a specific version.
steps.why: Specific praise helps people grow, because they know exactly what to keep doing.

steps.body: Give one colleague specific praise this week: what they did, and why it worked.

lessons.title: Feedback to Your Manager
lessons.summary: Upward feedback can be kind and useful.

steps.title: Managers need feedback too
steps.body: Most managers rarely hear honest feedback from their team. Sharing it kindly, about specific situations and how they affected your work, can help them lead better.

steps.prompt: Your manager often changes priorities at the last minute, and it’s causing stress. What’s the best way to raise it?

options.text: “Late priority changes make it hard to deliver. Could we plan the week on Mondays?”
options.why: Specific, focused on impact, and offers a solution.

options.text: Complain to colleagues instead.
options.why: It won’t change anything and may get back to them.

options.text: “You’re so disorganised.”
options.why: A personal label will make them defensive.

steps.prompt: Focus on the effect.
steps.why: Describing the effect on your work keeps the feedback fair and useful.

steps.prompt: Would you feel able to give your manager feedback?
steps.reply: Starting with something small and specific is the easiest way in.

steps.title: Your one-to-one

lines.text: Anything I could do differently to support you?

steps.prompt: Last-minute changes are stressing you. Reply:

options.text: No, all good!
options.why: A missed chance. They asked, and nothing will change.

options.text: Honestly? Last-minute changes are tough. Could we agree priorities each Monday?
options.reaction: That’s really helpful, let’s try it.
options.why: Specific, kind and practical, so it’s easy for them to act on.

options.text: Stop changing your mind all the time.
options.why: True, perhaps, but the tone makes it hard to hear.

steps.body: In your next one-to-one, share one specific, kind piece of feedback with your manager.

lessons.title: Receive Feedback Well
lessons.summary: Curiosity helps when feedback stings.

steps.title: The sting is normal
steps.body: Even fair feedback can sting, and the urge to defend yourself is natural. Pausing to get curious turns criticism into something you can use.

steps.prompt: Your manager says your weekly updates are “too brief”. What’s the best response?

options.text: Explain why each past update was fine.
options.why: Defending every point can look like you’re not listening, and you miss what they want.

options.text: “Thanks. Which details would make them more useful to you?”
options.why: A curious question gets you specifics, and shows you take the feedback seriously.

options.text: Decide your manager just doesn’t like you.
options.why: Jumping to that story can colour every future conversation with them.

steps.prompt: Ask for specifics.
steps.why: An example turns vague feedback into something you can act on straight away.

steps.prompt: When you get critical feedback, what’s your first reaction?
steps.reply: Your first reaction is fine. What helps is the curious question you ask next.

steps.prompt: Match each defensive reply with a better one.
steps.why: Curious replies keep feedback coming and help you improve, while defensive ones make people stop telling you.

steps.body: The next time you get feedback, thank them and ask one clarifying question before responding.

lessons.title: Ask for Feedback
lessons.summary: Don’t wait for your review to learn.

steps.title: Ask small and often
steps.body: Waiting for an annual review means waiting a year to improve. Asking “What’s one thing I could do better?” after a project gets you useful, low-pressure feedback right away.

steps.prompt: You just finished your first big presentation. How do you get useful feedback?

options.text: Wait to see if anyone says anything.
options.why: Most people won’t offer feedback unless asked.

options.text: “Was that okay?”
options.why: Too general. You’ll likely just get “yes, fine”.

options.text: Ask a colleague: “What’s one thing I could do better next time?”
options.why: A specific, small question makes it easy to give honest feedback.

steps.prompt: Ask for one thing.
steps.before: What’s one thing I could do
steps.why: Asking for just one thing makes honest feedback feel easy to give.

steps.prompt: Who could give you useful feedback right now?
steps.reply: Ask them one small question this week. It’s a quick way to grow.

steps.prompt: Gets useful feedback, or a vague answer?

cards.text: “What worked well, and what didn’t?”
“Was it good?”
“Was my opening clear enough?”
“Any thoughts?”
“What would you change if you did it?”

steps.why: Specific questions invite specific, honest answers, which are the ones you can actually use.

steps.body: After your next piece of work, ask one person: “What’s one thing I could do better?”

lessons.title: Handle Unfair Criticism
lessons.summary: Stay calm, find what’s useful, and respond clearly.

steps.title: Not all criticism is fair
steps.body: Sometimes feedback is unfair or badly delivered. Staying calm, finding any useful part, and then calmly sharing your side keeps your reputation strong.

steps.prompt: A colleague says in a meeting that your report “was full of mistakes”. You found one typo. What’s best?

options.text: “That’s not true!”
options.why: Reacting defensively in public can make you look worse.

options.text: “Thanks, I’d like to fix any mistakes. Could you show me which ones after this?”
options.why: Calm and open, and it moves the details somewhere you can respond fairly.

options.text: Say nothing and stew about it.
options.why: It may leave the wrong impression with others.

steps.prompt: Ask for specifics.
steps.before: Could you give me a specific
steps.why: Specifics turn vague criticism into something you can check and respond to.

steps.prompt: When criticism feels unfair, your first reaction is…
steps.reply: A calm question buys you time and usually shows what’s really going on.

steps.prompt: Responding to unfair criticism. Put these in order.
steps.why: Calm questions and fair acknowledgement make your correction far more credible.

steps.body: Next time feedback feels unfair, ask for a specific example before responding.

lessons.title: Repair a Team Tension
lessons.summary: Acknowledge impact and reset expectations.

steps.title: Quick repairs keep teams safe
steps.body: Small slips at work, like interrupting or a sharp email, can make colleagues hold back. A quick, simple repair keeps the team feeling safe to speak.

steps.prompt: During a team presentation, you talked over a teammate twice. You noticed them go quiet. What now?

options.text: Suggest they speak up more next time.
options.why: It puts the problem on them, when the interrupting came from you.

options.text: “I interrupted you earlier, sorry. Please finish your point.”
options.why: Owning it in the moment and handing the floor back repairs things quickly.

options.text: Avoid them for the rest of the week.
options.why: Avoidance lets awkwardness grow and can quietly harm how you work together.

steps.prompt: Hand the floor back.
steps.why: Giving the floor back shows respect and makes the apology real.

steps.prompt: Which small work slip do you find hardest to own?
steps.reply: Good to know. A quick, simple repair there will build a lot of goodwill.

steps.title: A short reply

lines.text: I think we should go with option B for the client.
Fine. Whatever you think is best.

steps.prompt: Leo had argued for option A. Reply:

options.text: Great, B it is then 👍
options.why: Taking “fine” at face value can leave a teammate quietly frustrated and disengaged.

options.text: That sounded like a not-so-fine “fine” 🙂 Can we chat about A? I want to get it right.
options.reaction: Ha, yeah. Thanks. I’ve got a couple of points on A.
options.why: You noticed the tension and invited them back in, which repairs it before it grows.

options.text: No need for the attitude.
options.why: Calling it out sharply makes them defensive and deepens the tension.

steps.body: After your next tense moment at work, make a brief repair within the same day.

lessons.title: Difficult Colleagues
lessons.summary: Work well with people you find hard.

steps.title: You don’t have to be friends
steps.body: Everyone works with someone they find difficult. You don’t need to like them, but staying professional, assuming good intent where you can, and keeping communication clear makes work easier.

steps.prompt: A colleague often replies to your messages abruptly, and it’s getting to you. What’s best?

options.text: Reply just as curtly.
options.why: Matching it escalates the tension.

options.text: “I sometimes find our messages a bit tense. Would a quick call be easier?”
options.why: Calm and solution-focused, and it opens the door to better communication.

options.text: Avoid working with them entirely.
options.why: Rarely possible, and it can slow everyone’s work.

steps.prompt: Assume good intent.
steps.why: A kinder explanation helps you stay calm and respond well.

steps.prompt: What makes a colleague hardest to work with, for you?
steps.reply: Naming it helps you plan a calm, professional response.

steps.prompt: Match each difficult behaviour with a calm response.
steps.why: Calm, specific responses keep work moving, whatever the other person brings.

steps.body: With a colleague you find difficult, try one calm, solution-focused message this week.

lessons.title: Clear the Air
lessons.summary: After a tense moment, reach out first.

steps.title: Tension grows in silence
steps.body: After a sharp exchange, it’s easy to avoid each other. A short, friendly message, or a quick chat, clears the air before it becomes a lasting problem.

steps.prompt: You and a teammate had a tense exchange in yesterday’s meeting. Today it feels awkward. What’s best?

options.text: “Hey, yesterday got a bit heated. Fancy a coffee and a reset?”
options.why: Light, friendly and direct, which makes it easy to move on.

options.text: Avoid them until it blows over.
options.why: Avoidance often makes awkwardness last longer.

options.text: Tell your manager about it.
options.why: Escalating before talking to them can damage trust.

steps.prompt: A friendly reset.
steps.why: Suggesting a reset shows you value the working relationship more than being right.

steps.prompt: After a tense moment at work, you usually…
steps.reply: Reaching out first is often all it takes to get back on track.

steps.title: The morning after

lines.text: Hey, yesterday’s meeting got a bit heated. Coffee and a reset?
Yeah… I was stressed and came across badly. Sorry.

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: Okay.
options.why: A flat reply leaves things a bit cold.

options.text: You did, a bit.
options.why: Agreeing with the criticism can reopen the tension.

options.text: Me too, honestly. Let’s grab that coffee and figure out the plan together.
options.why: You share responsibility and move straight to working together.

steps.body: If things feel awkward with a colleague after a tense moment, reach out first today.

lessons.title: Collaborate With Trust
lessons.summary: Make responsibilities visible and shared.

steps.title: Everyone’s job is no one’s job
steps.body: When ownership is fuzzy, tasks fall through the gaps and people quietly blame each other. Clear owners and deadlines protect both work and trust.

steps.prompt: You and a teammate each assumed the other would follow up with an important client. It’s been a week. What helps?

options.text: Agree who owns it, by when, and how you’ll confirm it’s done.
options.why: Clear ownership fixes this follow-up and stops the same gap happening again.

options.text: Assume someone will sort it eventually.
options.why: That’s how it slipped in the first place; the client may notice before anyone acts.

options.text: Post a vague “Can someone handle this?” in the team chat.
options.why: Group messages without an owner often get likes but no action.

steps.title: Who, what, by when
steps.body: End meetings by naming who does what, by when. It feels formal at first, but it saves so many awkward “I thought you were doing it” chats.

steps.prompt: Which shared task at work needs a clearer owner?
steps.placeholder: The task is… and the owner should be…

steps.prompt: Clear ownership, or an assumption?

cards.text: “I’ll email the client by Thursday.”
“Someone should follow up.”
Ending meetings by naming who does what
“I thought you were doing it.”
A shared list with names and dates

steps.why: Naming who owns each task is how teams avoid the gaps where everyone assumed someone else had it.

steps.body: Clarify the owner, next step and deadline for one shared task this week.

lessons.title: Share the Credit
lessons.summary: Generous credit builds a trusting team.

steps.title: Credit is a trust signal
steps.body: When something goes well, naming everyone who helped shows you’re fair and generous. People who share credit find others more willing to help them next time.

steps.prompt: Your director praises “your” project in a meeting. Two teammates did a lot of the work. What do you say?

options.text: “Thank you!” and leave it there.
options.why: Your teammates may feel their work went unseen.

options.text: “Thanks! Ravi built the dashboard and Lena ran the research. Real team effort.”
options.why: Naming specific contributions is fair and builds trust in the team.

options.text: “It was mostly me, to be honest.”
options.why: Taking credit others earned quickly erodes trust.

steps.prompt: Name who helped.
steps.why: Naming people specifically makes credit-sharing feel real, not just polite.

steps.prompt: How do you feel when someone credits your work?
steps.reply: Others feel the same, so sharing credit is one of the easiest ways to build trust.

steps.prompt: Shares credit, or takes it?

cards.text: “Huge thanks to Priya for the data.”
Presenting a colleague’s idea as yours
Copying helpers into the thank-you email
“I did most of it anyway.”
Telling their manager what they did well

steps.why: Sharing credit costs nothing and builds a team where people want to help each other.

steps.body: Next time your work is praised, name at least one person who helped.

lessons.title: Celebrate Team Wins
lessons.summary: Mark milestones together, not just deadlines.

steps.title: Wins deserve a moment
steps.body: Teams often rush from one deadline to the next. Pausing to celebrate a launch or a milestone, even with a quick shout-out or a coffee, keeps morale and connection high.

steps.prompt: Your team just hit a big quarterly goal. Everyone’s already onto the next thing. What’s best?

options.text: Move straight on. There’s a lot to do.
options.why: Skipping celebrations can make hard work feel unrewarded.

options.text: Suggest a team lunch and a quick round of thanks.
options.why: A small celebration shows the effort mattered and brings the team together.

options.text: Wait for management to organise something.
options.why: It may not happen. Anyone can start a celebration.

steps.prompt: Mark the moment.
steps.why: Naming the win and pausing to enjoy it boosts the whole team.

steps.prompt: How does your team celebrate wins?
steps.reply: Even a five-minute shout-out can make a real difference.

steps.prompt: Match each win with a way to celebrate.
steps.why: Celebrations matched to the moment show that every kind of effort is noticed.

steps.body: Suggest a small way to celebrate your team’s next win, however small.
